currentContext.business: Founded in 1998 and headquartered in Hyderabad, Rainbow operates a network of 24 hospitals and 5 clinics across 9 cities with over 2,435 beds dedicated to child-centric care. Pediatric services form the backbone, covering newborn and pediatric intensive care (PICU/NICU), multi-specialty treatments and advanced quaternary care such as multi-organ transplants, while Birthright handles routine and complex obstetric care, fetal medicine, perinatal genetics, IVF and gynecology. The Company serves children, mothers and families through an asset-light hub-and-spoke model, with about 50% of pediatric cases arriving as emergencies.

currentContext.expansion: Rainbow has grown into a network of 24 hospitals and 5 clinics across 9 cities, offering over 2,435 beds, expanded through an asset-light hub-and-spoke model. Large hub hospitals of around 200 plus beds (described elsewhere as at least 150 beds) at Banjara Hills (Hyderabad), Marathahalli (Bengaluru), Guindy (Chennai) and Malviya Nagar (Delhi) serve as centres for tertiary and quaternary care with specialized PICU/NICU units, while spoke hospitals of mostly 70+ beds (minimum 50 beds) provide secondary and tertiary services in nearby regions without full duplication of high-end facilities - a setup that improves bed utilization, balances service mix and cuts operational costs. Recent expansions include new units in Anna Nagar (Chennai), Rajahmundry, Electronic City, HRBR, Mahadevapura IVF, Warangal and Guwahati, and the model supports scalability with ongoing projects in Gurugram, Electronic City, Pune, Segualli and others. During FY2025-26 the Company completed two hospital acquisitions, expanding its geographic footprint and capacity in line with its growth strategy; post year-end it further strengthened the network by operationalising new hospital locations and launching an IVF centre, which management expects to support volume growth and improved infrastructure utilisation over the medium term. Management states that the expansion of the network during the year increased the operating base and strengthened the Company's ability to deploy capital efficiently across established and emerging markets, and that the operational expansion initiatives are expected to contribute to improved operational efficiencies, higher throughput and greater revenue visibility. Forward plans emphasise optimising existing units, targeted Tier II expansions via clinical models, IVF/maternity growth, an international push and M&A. No project-wise capex outlay, commissioning date or bed-addition schedule is disclosed in this section.

risks.risk: Medical ethics, legal and regulatory compliance
risks.note: Operating in a highly regulated sector requires consistent compliance with healthcare, labour, environmental, data and anti-corruption requirements; any breach can affect licenses, reputation and operating flexibility. Mitigated through a strengthened code of conduct, compliance training, whistle-blower mechanisms, internal controls, policy reviews, ethics oversight and periodic legal/compliance audits. Flagged as having negative financial implications.

Hospitals handle sensitive patient and employee data; any unauthorised access, leak or cyber incident can result in legal exposure, regulatory scrutiny, service disruption and loss of trust. Mitigated via access controls, encryption, privileged-access management, backup and recovery protocols, vendor safeguards, awareness training, incident response and regular security audits. Negative financial implications.

risks.risk: Occupational health and safety of clinical staff
risks.note: Clinical staff face exposure to infections, sharps injuries, chemicals, radiation, patient-handling risks and fire/emergency hazards; a strong safety culture is essential to protect employees and ensure uninterrupted patient care. Mitigated through infection prevention and control protocols, PPE, safety training, emergency drills, incident reporting, root-cause review, vaccination support, ergonomic controls and periodic health surveillance. Negative financial implications.

risks.risk: Water and waste management (hazardous and non-hazardous)
risks.note: Healthcare facilities generate biomedical, hazardous and domestic waste and are significant users of water; weak segregation, treatment or reuse practices can lead to non-compliance, reputational damage, infection risk and higher operating cost. Mitigated through strict segregation and labeling, authorised disposal via approved vendors, wastewater treatment and reuse, rainwater harvesting where feasible, 3R practices and periodic audits against pollution control requirements. Negative financial implications.

risks.risk: Responsible procurement and supply chain resilience
risks.note: Uninterrupted availability of medicines, consumables, diagnostics and equipment is critical in healthcare; poor supplier governance or concentration risk can affect service delivery and cost stability. Mitigation includes supplier due diligence, quality and ethical sourcing checks, critical inventory planning and an alternate sourcing strategy. Negative financial implications.

risks.risk: Enterprise risk management and business continuity
risks.note: The healthcare business is exposed to operational, clinical, regulatory, technology, supply and external shocks; a structured risk management framework is needed to reduce disruption and protect continuity of care. Mitigated by enterprise risk registers, mitigation-plan reviews with stakeholders, monitoring of critical dependencies, stress-testing of business continuity and disaster recovery plans, and periodic management reviews. Negative financial implications.

risks.risk: Talent attraction, retention and high employee attrition
risks.note: Healthcare quality depends on the availability of skilled doctors, nurses, technicians and support staff. The BRSR discloses a permanent-employee turnover rate of 37% in FY2026 (34% male, 40% female), up from 35% in FY2025 and 33% in FY2024, with the Company noting FY2025-26 attrition data includes nursing exits with tenure of less than 3 months - a structural workforce-churn exposure for a consultant-led clinical model.

100% of turnover comes from a single activity - human health activities / medical services (healthcare services) - and operations are confined to six states in India with no international locations and no export revenue, leaving the Company undiversified by both business line and geography.

Hospital operations are energy-intensive because of continuous clinical services, critical equipment, HVAC loads, lighting and imaging systems; the Company frames improving energy efficiency as an opportunity (positive implications) addressed through energy audits, LED retrofits, smart metering, HVAC optimisation, preventive maintenance, renewable energy sourcing where feasible and site-level monitoring of utility intensity.

one-line thesis: Rainbow delivered record Q4 revenue (INR 460cr, +24% YoY) and PAT (+38% YoY) driven by 500 bed additions and recovering occupancies, with management guiding for 20% growth in FY27 fueled by a massive 900-bed pipeline (Gurugram, Coimbatore, Pune) and a strategic pivot to reduce seasonality via super-specialty mix and fertility expansion.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 460cr (Q4, +24% YoY), INR 1,703cr (FY26, +12% YoY); EBITDA: INR 145cr (Q4, +26% YoY), Margin 31.5% (Q4) / 32% (FY26); PAT: INR 78.2cr (Q4, +38% reported, +17% ex-deferred tax), INR 282cr (FY26, +15.3%); Order Book: ~900 beds in execution (Gurugram 450 beds, Coimbatore 130, Pune 150, Indore 100, Bangalore 80); Net Debt: Nil (Cash ~INR 600-700cr). One-offs: Q4 PAT boosted by deferred tax adjustments; FY26 growth muted by weak seasonal volume (typically 10-12% of top line) and geopolitical impact on international patients (Bangladesh/Somalia).
guidance: Revenue Growth: ~20% for FY27; Margins: Maintain current levels (~32% EBITDA) despite new ramp-ups; Order Inflow: Focus on converting leads via new CRM; Capex: INR 400-500cr for Gurugram + INR 300-350cr for other projects (Coimbatore, Pune, Indore) over next 2 years; Commissioning: Coimbatore (H2 FY28), Gurugram Sector 56 (H2 FY28), Gurugram Sector 44 (Q1 FY29), Pune (H2 FY28), Indore (~2 years).
order book & pipeline: ~900 beds in various stages: Gurugram (450 beds total: 125 in Sector 56, 325 in Sector 44); Coimbatore (130 beds); Pune (150 beds); Indore (100 beds build-to-suit); Bangalore Seegehalli (80 beds). Total investment est. INR 700-850cr over 2.5 years.
segment / subsidiary detail: Pediatrics: Largest chain in India, expanding super-specialties (liver/bone marrow transplants); Obstetrics: ~32% of revenue mix (up from 28-30%); Fertility (IVF): INR 61.4cr in FY26 (3.7% of rev), growing 25% YoY, now 4.1% in Q4; International Patients: Flat at INR 28.9cr due to geopolitical disruptions.
growth verticals / optionality: M&A strategy targeting assets >50 beds with scale to 100+; New geographies (emerging cities); Deepening specialty stack in Bangalore/Chennai to match Hyderabad; Fertility center expansion; Indore management contract transitioning to owned/leased asset.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA margin stable at 32% despite new capacity; Pharmacy cost ~12-13% of revenue (not disclosed separately); ALOS stable at 2.7 days (clinical reality, not manageable lower); Occupancy target 56-58% for optimal economics (Q4 at 45.3%, mature units ~52%).
capex / expansion: FY26 Capex: INR 217cr; Q4 Capex: INR 61cr; Future Capex: INR 400-500cr (Gurugram own-land) + INR 300-350cr (Leased/Build-to-suit: Coimbatore, Pune, Indore, Bangalore); Intensity: INR 65-70 lakhs/bed for non-Gurugram projects; Maintenance Capex: ~INR 45cr/year.
capital allocation: 100% internal accruals funding for all expansion; No debt planned; Cash reserves ~INR 600-700cr; Dividend policy not explicitly detailed but balance sheet remains conservative with zero leverage.
risks & watch-items: Seasonality dependence (though reducing); Execution risk on 900-bed pipeline; Geopolitical impact on international patient inflow; Talent acquisition for super-specialties in new cities; Regulatory approvals for greenfield projects.
management quality / tone: Confident and aggressive on capacity addition; Pragmatic on seasonality headwinds; Data-driven focus on occupancy and conversion (new CEO pushing CRM/HIS); Clear distinction from 'mom-and-pop' competitors emphasizing clinical depth.
non-obvious takeaways: Indore deal structure: Rainbow manages pediatric/OB units in existing 200-bed multi-specialty hospital (25 ICU beds dedicated) while partner builds adjacent 100-bed dedicated facility for Rainbow to move into in 2 years; Revenue booked directly by Rainbow, not O&M fee; ALOS of 2.7 days is a hard clinical floor for pediatric/obs, not an efficiency lever.

themes.title: Hospitals, diagnostics & domestic healthcare
themes.need: Under-bedded India plus insurance penetration and preventive-care adoption drive a domestic healthcare capex + volume cycle distinct from export pharma. MAXHEALTH adding ~2,500+ beds (Gurgaon 500-bed by FY27); APOLLOHOSP/MEDANTA/KIMS/NH/ASTERDM/MAXHEALTH on hospitals; LALPATHLAB/METROPOLIS/THYROCARE/VIJAYA on diagnostics (LALPATHLAB guides 13-15% FY27); MEDPLUS/ENTERO on pharmacy/distribution; POLYMED on devices. The same India-only demand engine now also carries India-facing branded pharma, which is driven by domestic volume and price rather than the export book: GLAXO delivered its first INR 1,000cr quarter with 8.1% revenue growth, Shingrix at a ~INR 75cr annual run-rate (CY25, +80% YoY) and Jemperli's first-line approval expanding eligible patients from 800 to 6,000; ERIS (dermatology 15% of revenue after INR 1,265cr of domestic brand acquisitions), SANOFI (India-for-India, NLEM price cuts) and THEMISMED (hospital segment +20% YoY) sit on the same axis.
themes.driver: New-bed commissioning + occupancy ramp; Tier 3/4 diagnostics penetration; CGHS rate revision; preventive-test volumes; domestic branded-formulation volume growth and NLEM/price actions.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Rainbow Children's Medicare Limited is a leading Indian provider of specialized pediatric and perinatal care, running an integrated mother-and-child hospital network under the Rainbow Children's Hospital and Birthright by Rainbow brands.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Founded in 1998 and headquartered in Hyderabad, Rainbow operates a network of 24 hospitals and 5 clinics across 9 cities with over 2,435 beds dedicated to child-centric care. Pediatric services form the backbone, covering newborn and pediatric intensive care (PICU/NICU), multi-specialty treatments and advanced quaternary care such as multi-organ transplants, while Birthright handles routine and complex obstetric care, fetal medicine, perinatal genetics, IVF and gynecology. The Company serves children, mothers and families through an asset-light hub-and-spoke model, with about 50% of pediatric cases arriving as emergencies.

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body: Pediatrics: Largest chain in India, expanding super-specialties (liver/bone marrow transplants); Obstetrics: ~32% of revenue mix (up from 28-30%); Fertility (IVF): INR 61.4cr in FY26 (3.7% of rev), growing 25% YoY, now 4.1% in Q4; International Patients: Flat at INR 28.9cr due to geopolitical disruptions.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Pediatric care:** Rainbow Children's Hospital
- **Women's healthcare / perinatal:** Birthright by Rainbow

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- Domestic Indian pediatric and maternal healthcare patients across nine cities and six states
- Tier II Indian cities targeted for expansion via clinical models
- International / medical-tourism patients from Bangladesh, Bhutan, Bahrain, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Somalia, Sudan and the Maldives
- NRIs travelling to India for cost-competitive healthcare

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body: ~900 beds in various stages: Gurugram (450 beds total: 125 in Sector 56, 325 in Sector 44); Coimbatore (130 beds); Pune (150 beds); Indore (100 beds build-to-suit); Bangalore Seegehalli (80 beds). Total investment est. INR 700-850cr over 2.5 years.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue Growth: ~20% for FY27; Margins: Maintain current levels (~32% EBITDA) despite new ramp-ups; Order Inflow: Focus on converting leads via new CRM; Capex: INR 400-500cr for Gurugram + INR 300-350cr for other projects (Coimbatore, Pune, Indore) over next 2 years; Commissioning: Coimbatore (H2 FY28), Gurugram Sector 56 (H2 FY28), Gurugram Sector 44 (Q1 FY29), Pune (H2 FY28), Indore (~2 years).

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: M&A strategy targeting assets >50 beds with scale to 100+; New geographies (emerging cities); Deepening specialty stack in Bangalore/Chennai to match Hyderabad; Fertility center expansion; Indore management contract transitioning to owned/leased asset.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Management expects new hospitals maturing and strengthened digital capabilities driving patient engagement to position Rainbow to reinforce its leadership in specialized women's and children's healthcare
- A significant phase of planned capacity additions is now operational, so the near-term lever is higher utilization and occupancy rather than fresh capacity, particularly across recently commissioned and acquired hospitals
- Successful integration and strong performance of recent acquisitions has reinforced management confidence in pursuing similar opportunities
- The consultant-led model, deep expertise in pediatrics and perinatal care and commitment of teams across the network are cited by the CEO as the standout operating strengths
- India's real GDP growth for FY2026-27 is projected between 6.8% and 7.2% (Crisil forecasts 6.6%), supported by government infrastructure spending, steadily rising private investment and a reliable services growth path
- India's healthcare expenditure was 3.3% of GDP in 2023, among the lowest in the world, with per capita healthcare expenditure of $84.7 - only 11.1% of China's - indicating a structurally under-served market
- India lags the global average in hospital bed availability against the IPHS desirable benchmark of 20 beds per 10,000 population (10 beds per 10,000 the minimum essential standard)
- Structural demand drivers cited for India: demographic dividend (working-age population of 849.9 million in 2023, peaking at 967.7 million in 2034), rising urbanization (urban population to reach 567.7 million by 2030, 37.2% of total) and growing per capita income (CAGR of 6.6% between FY2023 and FY2026)
- Private consumption continues to anchor India's economic growth, with PFCE growth of 7.7% between FY2025 and FY2026 supported by GST rate rationalization, stable employment and rising real purchasing power
- Downside risks to the macro outlook include escalation of geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, a reevaluation of AI profit expectations leading to lower investment, abrupt financial-market correction, and larger fiscal deficits pressuring long-term interest rates

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: EBITDA margin stable at 32% despite new capacity; Pharmacy cost ~12-13% of revenue (not disclosed separately); ALOS stable at 2.7 days (clinical reality, not manageable lower); Occupancy target 56-58% for optimal economics (Q4 at 45.3%, mature units ~52%).

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: 100% internal accruals funding for all expansion; No debt planned; Cash reserves ~INR 600-700cr; Dividend policy not explicitly detailed but balance sheet remains conservative with zero leverage.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Rainbow has grown into a network of 24 hospitals and 5 clinics across 9 cities, offering over 2,435 beds, expanded through an asset-light hub-and-spoke model. Large hub hospitals of around 200 plus beds (described elsewhere as at least 150 beds) at Banjara Hills (Hyderabad), Marathahalli (Bengaluru), Guindy (Chennai) and Malviya Nagar (Delhi) serve as centres for tertiary and quaternary care with specialized PICU/NICU units, while spoke hospitals of mostly 70+ beds (minimum 50 beds) provide secondary and tertiary services in nearby regions without full duplication of high-end facilities - a setup that improves bed utilization, balances service mix and cuts operational costs. Recent expansions include new units in Anna Nagar (Chennai), Rajahmundry, Electronic City, HRBR, Mahadevapura IVF, Warangal and Guwahati, and the model supports scalability with ongoing projects in Gurugram, Electronic City, Pune, Segualli and others. During FY2025-26 the Company completed two hospital acquisitions, expanding its geographic footprint and capacity in line with its growth strategy; post year-end it further strengthened the network by operationalising new hospital locations and launching an IVF centre, which management expects to support volume growth and improved infrastructure utilisation over the medium term. Management states that the expansion of the network during the year increased the operating base and strengthened the Company's ability to deploy capital efficiently across established and emerging markets, and that the operational expansion initiatives are expected to contribute to improved operational efficiencies, higher throughput and greater revenue visibility. Forward plans emphasise optimising existing units, targeted Tier II expansions via clinical models, IVF/maternity growth, an international push and M&A. No project-wise capex outlay, commissioning date or bed-addition schedule is disclosed in this section.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident and aggressive on capacity addition; Pragmatic on seasonality headwinds; Data-driven focus on occupancy and conversion (new CEO pushing CRM/HIS); Clear distinction from 'mom-and-pop' competitors emphasizing clinical depth.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Innovative hub-and-spoke model: large central hubs act as main centres for secondary, tertiary and top-level specialty care while spokes serve nearby regions, improving bed utilisation, balancing service mix and keeping costs in check
- Strong brand identity in pediatric healthcare, drawing patients and doctor recommendations across regions and building deep trust and loyalty so families return for all their healthcare needs
- Excellence in pediatric and perinatal care with expert services in neurology, nephrology, oncology and cardiology; skill in blending children's and newborn care sets it apart and gives a clear market edge
- Child-centric healthcare framework - friendly hospital spaces and staff specially trained to comfort children, leading to better treatment results and happier patients
- Collaborative multi-disciplinary approach bringing pediatrics, neurology, nephrology, oncology and cardiology experts together with nurses, therapists and admin staff for personalized treatment plans
- Strategic doctor engagement: over 1,050+ full-time doctors on retainer for 24/7 consultant-led care (elsewhere stated as over 910 full-time doctors), many with advanced training from the UK, USA, Canada and Australia
- Runs India's largest private pediatric Diplomate of National Board (DNB) training program with postgraduate and fellowship spots, building a pipeline of future specialists
- Integrated mother-and-child ecosystem creating seamless care from pregnancy through neonatal stages to advanced pediatric needs, boosting patient loyalty and positioning Rainbow as a top referral centre for critical cases
- COSO-aligned risk management framework with Risk Management Committee oversight and compliance training

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Seasonality dependence (though reducing); Execution risk on 900-bed pipeline; Geopolitical impact on international patient inflow; Talent acquisition for super-specialties in new cities; Regulatory approvals for greenfield projects.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Indore deal structure: Rainbow manages pediatric/OB units in existing 200-bed multi-specialty hospital (25 ICU beds dedicated) while partner builds adjacent 100-bed dedicated facility for Rainbow to move into in 2 years; Revenue booked directly by Rainbow, not O&M fee; ALOS of 2.7 days is a hard clinical floor for pediatric/obs, not an efficiency lever.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Replicate the success of the Hyderabad flagship referral centre at the Bengaluru, Chennai, Gurugram and Guwahati flagship centres over the next five years, with the hub-and-spoke network and regional spoke hospitals complementing and accelerating growth of these referral centres
- Expand not merely to increase capacity but to make specialized women's and children's healthcare more accessible: strengthen South India leadership across Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu; build a meaningful presence across the National Capital Region and its surrounding growth corridors in North …

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Acquisitions] The 2025-2026 phase covers the "Acquisition of: Prashanthi Hospital, Warangal & Pratiksha Hospital, Guwahati", with footnotes dating Prashanthi (100 beds) to 1st July 2025 within Telangana and the Guwahati 150 beds to "acquisition & integration of Pratiksha Hospital, Guwahati from 1st September 2025"; both sit in the "New Hospitals" (under 5 years) bucket.
- [Doctor model] Doctors "work exclusively on a full-time, retainer basis" in teams with a 24/7 commitment, supported by "Retainer/Support in beginning years", competitive compensation and absorption into the network - the stated source of "High retention and loyalty" and support for pediatric retrieval services.
- [Ownership] Shareholding as on June 30, 2026: Promoter & Promoter Group 49.8%, MFs & AIFs 19.9%, FPIs & NRIs 16.0%, Others 14.3%; institutional holders above 1% include ICICI Prudential & ISIF Equity Fund (5.9%), DSP Mutual Fund (4.1%), Franklin Templeton Investment Funds (2.9%), Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (2.1%) and Vanguard Fund (1.9%).
- [Clinical capability] The appendix details capability the deck presents as competitive depth: a pediatric ECMO retrieval team that travelled ~1,800 km to Guwahati for "the first reported pediatric ECMO transfer out of Northeast India" (child on ECMO 36 days, discharged in good health); multi-organ trauma management after a five-storey fall; a hemispherotomy for drug-refractory epilepsy; and a chronic Caesarean Scar Ectopic Pregnancy repair - the ECMO case framed as "expanding the addressable referral base and reinforcing the hospital's role as a national escalation point for pediatric critical care".
- [Capex character] The deck notes "Allocation of significant portion of capex towards interiors of hospitals for creating congenial environment", tying spend to the child-centric design premise, but gives no capex amount.
